clue.text: London writer at home after skating — bureaucratic type

indicators.note: after places the skating piece behind the writer and the at-home piece

parts.note: Jack London was the American author of The Call of the Wild
in means at home, as in 'is she in?'
off ice: someone who has finished skating is off the ice

explanation.surface: A London author relaxes at home after a session at the rink, then turns out to be a petty official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London writer' looks like a Londoner, but it is Jack London. 'Skating' gives OFF ICE, the state after skating.
explanation.definitionFit: A jack-in-office is an old idiom for a self-important minor official who enjoys petty authority.

clue.text: Mooniest of gods

parts.note: among the planets named after Roman deities, the one king of the gods has the greatest number of moons

explanation.definitionFit: The planet named for the chief Roman deity has more known satellites than the other gas giants did when this was set, a fact turned into a coined superlative.

clue.text: Music-maker needs source of electricity, love

parts.note: a cell is a battery unit producing electric current
love is nil in tennis, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A musician says all they require is a power supply and some affection.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowed string instrument played between the knees produces music, so it is a maker of music.

clue.text: Isn't given trouble when buying shares

indicators.note: trouble means to stir up or disturb, so these letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone is not troubled at all while purchasing stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' reworks the letters of ISNT GIVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting money into stocks in the hope of profit is the commonest kind of financial placement of funds.

clue.text: Work addressed to a Manx cat ?

parts.note: O is the old vocative used when calling on someone, as in 'O Lord'

indicators.note: the Manx breed has no tail, so the cat word loses its final letter

parts.note: puss is a familiar name for a cat

explanation.surface: A poem written to a tailless cat from the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manx' signals a missing tail because the Isle of Man breed of cat is born tailless; the O is the old form of address, as in 'O Lord'.
explanation.definitionFit: Opus is Latin for a work, used of a numbered musical composition.

clue.text: A flat? It's sadly my lot, he says

indicators.note: sadly suggests things gone wrong, so these letters are disarranged

explanation.surface: A tenant resigned to a poor apartment sighs that it is simply their fate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges A FLAT ITS. The definition is the kind of person who would say 'it's my lot'.
explanation.definitionFit: One who believes everything is predetermined accepts whatever fate deals and calls it their destiny.

clue.text: Troll (for) this

parts.note: a troll is an old word for a round sung by several voices, and trolling (for) is fishing with a moving line for what you hope to land

explanation.definitionFit: A round song and a haul of fish share this word: a troll is such a song, and anglers troll for a haul.

clue.text: No membership in this body? Well, I'm blessed!

indicators.note: the words that follow form the body in which the letters sit, so they are tucked inside that exclamation

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at a club with no members.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the last L of 'Well' through 'blessed'. Members here are arms and legs, not club members.
explanation.definitionFit: Limbs are the body's members, so a body lacking them has no membership in that anatomical sense.

clue.text: A 'study may change to this sanctum, say

indicators.note: change tells us to rearrange the letters, with those of the final word taken out of the mix

explanation.surface: A scholar's room might be converted into a private holy place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges A STUDY MAY; remove the letters of SAY and the rest give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient temples the innermost shrine, open only to priests, was a sacred inner room.

clue.text: But the record jump exceeds 16 feet

definitions.text: But the record jump exceeds 16 feet

parts.words: But the record jump exceeds 16 feet
parts.note: describes an athletics event where competitors clear a bar with a pole, the record then standing above sixteen and a half feet

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 16 and a half feet, the world record at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: An athletics jump using a long flexible pole to clear a high bar is the event whose record passed that height.

clue.text: Sound advice to a would-be vendor or three

indicators.note: sound means the words are heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: someone hoping to sell is told to try an ad

explanation.surface: A seller gets a tip on how to shift goods, or perhaps three tips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' also passes for 'reliable', as in sound advice.
explanation.definitionFit: A triad is a group or set of three.

clue.text: Among ratings love is a religion

indicators.note: among puts the following pieces in the midst of the ratings word

parts.note: TAM, Television Audience Measurement, was the British TV ratings system of the 1950s and 60s
love is nil in tennis, written as the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sermon-like claim that love is a creed even among sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ratings' suggests sailors, but here it is TAM, the old British television audience figures.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chinese philosophy of the Way, founded on Lao-tzu's teachings, is also practised as a faith.

clue.text: Roman has followed a record of all the characters

indicators.note: followed puts the Latin verb after the record

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record
habet is Latin for 'he has', so a Roman would say it

explanation.surface: A Roman has followed a record listing every character in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman has' is Latin: HABET means 'he has'. 'Characters' are letters, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: The full set of letters used in writing a language, from A to Z.

clue.text: A bird that's just joined the army

definitions.text: A bird that's just joined the army

parts.words: A bird that's just joined the army
parts.note: a crow-family bird name plus a little more becomes slang for a raw recruit

explanation.definitionFit: A rookie is slang for a new recruit, with the name of a black crow-like bird at its start.

clue.text: New oil grand chief, one of few in power

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of oil are made afresh in a new order

parts.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
arch means chief, as in archenemy

explanation.surface: A new oil tycoon becomes a top boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges OIL to OLI.
explanation.definitionFit: An oligarchy is rule by a small group, and each member is a ruler among that elite few.

clue.text: No degree of change on this line

definitions.text: No degree of change on this line

parts.words: No degree of change on this line
parts.note: a map line joining places with the same temperature, so moving along it shows no shift in degrees

explanation.definitionFit: On weather maps, a line connecting points of equal temperature shows no variation in degrees along it.

clue.text: In commerce Jack's most versatile

parts.note: a jack of all trades is versatile, and the superlative of that in business is a shopkeeper

explanation.definitionFit: A shopkeeper or skilled worker deals in trades, punning on the jack of all trades.

clue.text: Sailor Bill sticks to the ship

definitions.text: Sailor Bill sticks to the ship

parts.words: Sailor Bill sticks to the ship
parts.note: ... Bill the Sailor is a bawdy folk song hero, and the crustacean of his name clings to hulls

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barnacle Bill the Sailor' is an old sea song.
explanation.definitionFit: The shellfish that clings to ship hulls also names the sailor of the song.

clue.text: Go wrong, consuming bad gin, or fish

indicators.note: consuming means eating up, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: to stray is to go wrong

indicators.note: bad means gone off, so these letters are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone drinking poor gin goes off the rails, or else goes fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' is the anagram signal for the gin, and 'consuming' puts the result inside the word for going wrong; 'or' is just a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat ray with a venomous barb on its tail is a kind of sea creature.

clue.text: African Scene a painter has put up

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means the letters run upward

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a painter

explanation.surface: An artist has hung a picture of an African landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses A RA HAS, reading upward in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The great desert of North Africa is a landscape typical of that continent.

clue.text: A long way. to equality before second half

indicators.note: before places the equality word ahead of the second piece

parts.note: par means equality, as in 'on a par'

indicators.note: half takes the first half of the word second

explanation.surface: A long journey toward evenness, with a second half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second half' gives SEC, the first half of SECOND.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of astronomical distance of about 3.26 light years, a long way indeed.

clue.text: " In sad —— let me be laid " (T. Night)

definitions.text: In sad —— let me be laid " (T. Night)

parts.words: In sad —— let me be laid " (T. Night)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word from Feste's song in Twelfth Night, 'Come away, death'

explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Shakespeare's Twelfth Night: 'Come away, come away, death, And in sad ___ let me be laid'.
explanation.definitionFit: The evergreen tree, symbol of mourning, fills the gap in Feste's song.

clue.text: News announcer familiar to palmists

definitions.meaning: the top line in a newspaper announcing a story
one of the creases on the palm that palm readers interpret

explanation.surface: A newsreader turns out to be well known to fortune-tellers.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's top line announces a story, and palm readers read a crease of the hand linked to the intellect.

clue.text: Hare racing about sun-rise

indicators.note: rise in a down clue means the pieces read upward

parts.note: re means about, concerning
sol is Latin for sun

explanation.surface: A hare speeds around at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' reverses both pieces, reading upward in a down clue. The definition rests on the fable: the hare famously lost its race to the tortoise.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fable the hare is beaten by the tortoise, making it the defeated party.

clue.text: Friend married, in retrospect, a bit of a cow

indicators.note: looking back means the combined letters read in reverse order

parts.note: pal is a friend
wed means married

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a friend who married, and who was a bit of a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retrospect' reverses PAL WED. 'Cow' looks like an insult but means the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The loose fold of skin hanging from the throat of cattle.

clue.text: Nothing doing at this end

parts.note: the idiom 'at a ___ end' means having nothing to do

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom at a loose end means idle, with nothing to occupy one.

clue.text: A penny on Pixie to make lots of lolly

indicators.note: on, in a down clue, places the penny above the fairy

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for a penny
an elf is a pixie

explanation.surface: A penny given to a fairy turns into a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lolly' is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelf is an old, disparaging word for money or riches.

clue.text: But a girl's not stony with plenty of these

definitions.text: But a girl's not stony with plenty of these

parts.words: But a girl's not stony with plenty of these
parts.note: stony means broke, and a girl laden with diamonds, slang for gems, is far from broke

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony' is short for stony broke, British for penniless. The word means both stones and diamonds.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for diamonds or jewels, a word that also means stones.

clue.text: West came over with new sort of paper

indicators.note: new tells us to make the letters afresh in a different order

explanation.surface: A Westerner came over with some new stationery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges W CAME OVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream-wove is a smooth cream-coloured writing paper with no laid lines.

clue.text: Inexperienced with the four-in-hand, but useful in the garden

parts.note: green means inexperienced
the four digits of a hand besides the thumb

explanation.surface: A novice coachman is hopeless with a team of four horses, but good at gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Four-in-hand' is a four-horse carriage, but here means the four digits.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a natural talent for making plants grow is the gardener's gift.
